## Bivariate distributions \[DS 3.4\] \[Lec 9\] {#sec:bivar-distr}

So far, we have mainly dealt with one random variable at a time. Let's
expand our toolset to deal with two or more variables at a time. First,
let's define a *bivariate* random vector of $X$ and $Y$.

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
**Bivariate random vector.**

$(X,Y): \Omega_{(X,Y)} \to \bR^2$.
:::

Just like in one variable's distribution (which has a cdf and pmf or pdf
associated with it), a bivariate random vector $(X,Y)$ also has a
distribution that describes its *joint* random behavior.

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
**Joint distribution.**

The joint distribution is defined as the collection of all probabilities
of the form $\mathbb{P}((X,Y) \in E)$ for all $E \subset \bR^2$ such
that $\{(X,Y)
  \in E\}$ is an event.
:::

We will start with the case where $X$ and $Y$ are both discrete, noting
that all of the following are possible:

-   $X$ and $Y$ are both discrete.

-   $X$ and $Y$ are both continuous.

-   $X$ is discrete, and $Y$ is continuous.

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
**Discrete joint distribution.**

When both $X$ and $Y$ are discrete, we say that $(X,Y)$ have a discrete
joint distribution (of only countably many possible values).
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Example"}
Suppose that $3$ balls are chosen at random from an urn with 4 red balls
and 3 blue balls. Call $X$ the number of red balls you will draw, and
$Y$ is the number of blue balls you will draw.

-   Are $X$ and $Y$ independent?

-   What are the possible values of $(X,Y)$ that have nonzero
    probability?

-   What is the probability that you will draw $2$ red balls and $1$
    blue ball?
:::

This naturally leads us to the notion of the *joint pmf* that describes
the probabilities of *all* such configurations of $X$ and $Y$.

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
**Joint pmf.**

The joint probability mass function (pmf) of $X$ and $Y$ is defined as
the function $f$ such that $$f(x,y) = \mathbb{P}(X=x,Y=y)$$ for all
$(x,y) \in \bR^2$.
:::

::: center
![image](figures/ds-figure-3-10-discrete-bivariate.png){width=".5\\linewidth"}
:::

The following two properties hold (these are analogous properties to the
ones you learned from single random variables' pmfs):

-   $f(x,y) \ge 0$ for all $(x,y)$, and

-   $\sum \nolimits_{(x,y)} f(x,y) = 1$.

(Hint: these can serve as a *sanity check* for your own pmfs.)

The joint pmf of two discrete random variables is a nonnegative function
$f$ such that the probability of the pair $(X, Y )$ being in a set $E$
is the sum of $f(x, y)$ over all points in $E$. A joint pmf can be
strictly positive at countably many pairs $(x, y)$ at most.

::: {.callout-tip title="Example"}
**Auto insurance.**

An auto insurance company uses the following joint following joint pmf
of $X$ (the brand of the car), and $Y$ (whether or not the car will be
stolen) for its actuarial calculations.

::: center
   Stolen    Brand 1   Brand 2   Brand 3   Brand 4   Brand 5   Total
  --------- --------- --------- --------- --------- --------- -------
   No (0)     0.129     0.298     0.161     0.280     0.108    0.976
   Yes (1)    0.010     0.010     0.001     0.002     0.001    0.024
    Total     0.139     0.308     0.162     0.282     0.109    1.000
:::

With the joint pmf, we can answer the following questions. (Write these
in terms of $X$ and $Y$, and find them)

-   What is the probability of a car being stolen?

-   What is the probability of a Brand 3 car being stolen?
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Example"}
**Auto insurance.**

A competing auto insurance company uses a different joint distribution
table. They still use the *overall*[^1] probabilities of brands ($X$)
and ($Y$):

$$f_X(x) = \mathbb{P}(X=x) =
\begin{cases}
0.139 &\text{ if }x=1\\
 0.308& \text{ if }x=2\\
 0.162& \text{ if }x=3\\
0.282& \text{ if }x=4\\
 0.109& \text{ if }x=5\\
 0& \text{ otherwise }
  \end{cases}\;\;\;\;\;
f_Y(y) =
\mathbb{P}(Y=y) =
\begin{cases}
0.0976 &\text{ if } y=0\\
0.024 &\text{ if } y =1\\
0 &\text{ otherwise.}
\end{cases}$$ However, in their actuarial calculations, this company
assumes that $X$ and $Y$ are *independent*[^2] In this case, what is
$P(X=1, Y=2)$ (Can you recognize how to make an entire joint pmf table
for this company?)
:::

Next, we will consider two *continuous* random variables $X$ and $Y$.

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
**Continuous joint distribution.**

We say that random variables $X$ and $Y$ have a continuous joint
distribution if both $X$ and $Y$ are continuous, and there exists a
nonnegative function $f$ defined over the entire xy-plane such that for
every subset $C$ of the plane,
$$\mathbb{P}((X,Y) \in C) = \iint_C f(x,y) dx dy.$$
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
**Joint pdf.**

The function $f$ defined above is the joint probability density function
(pdf).
:::

::: center
![image](figures/ds-figure-3-11-continuous-bivariate.png){width=".6\\linewidth"}
:::

The following two properties hold for any joint pdf $f$:

-   $f(x,y) \ge 0$ for all $(x,y) \in \bR^2$, and

-   $\iint_{\bR^2} f(x,y)\; dx dy = 1$.

We'll try a couple of examples next.

::: {.callout-tip title="Example"}
Suppose the joint pdf of $(X,Y)$ is
$f(x,y) = c x^2y \times 1_{ x^2 \le y <1}$.

-   Find $c$.

-   Calculate $\mathbb{P}(X>Y)$.

-   Calculate $\mathbb{P}(X=Y)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Example"}
Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are both $\text{Uniform}(0,1)$ independently. Let
$$Z=\lfloor{X/Y}\rfloor,$$ be the *floor* of the ratio $X/Y$ (i.e., $X$
divided by $Y$ then rounded down). Write the probability
$\mathbb{P}(Z=1)$ as an integral of the joint pdf and evaluate the
integral.
:::

**Bivariate Normal distribution.**

Occasionally, we run into scenarios where a *mixed* bivariate
distribution -- where one of the random variables is discrete and the
other is continuous -- comes in handy.

For example, let $X$ be the indicator of whether or not the first
patient is a "success" (no relapse). That is, $X=1$ if the patient does
not relapse and $X= 0$ if the patient relapses. Also, let $Y$ be the
proportion of patients who have no relapse among all patients who might
receive the treatment. It is clear that $X$ must have a discrete
distribution, but it might be sensible to think of $Y$ as a continuous
random variable taking its value anywhere in the interval $[0, 1]$.

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
**Mixed bivariate distribution.**

If $X$ is discrete, while $Y$ is continuous (or the other way around),
then $X$ and $Y$ follow a mixed bivariate distribution.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
**Joint pmf/pdf.**

A joint pmf/pdf is defined as the function $f(x,y)$ such that
$$\mathbb{P}(X \in A, Y \in B) =
  \int \nolimits_B \left[\sum\nolimits_{x\in A}f(x,y) \right]dy$$
:::

In words, the joint pdf of a discrete random variable $X$ and a
continuous random variable $Y$ is a nonnegative function $f$ such that
the probability of the pair $(X, Y )$ being in a set $E$ is obtained by
(1) summing $f(x, y)$ over all $x$ such that $(x, y) \in E$ for each $y$
and then (2) integrating the resulting function of $y$.

**Q:** Is the inside of the integral in the expression for
$\mathbb{P}(X \in A, Y \in B)$ a function of $y$ or not?

Every joint pmf/pdf $f$ (of discrete $X$ and continuous $Y$) must
satisfy the following properties:

-   $f(x,y) \ge 0$ for all $(x,y) \in \bR^2$, and

-   $\sum_{x} \int\nolimits_{-\infty}^\infty  f(x,y)dy = 1$.

::: {.callout-tip title="Example"}
Suppose that the joint pmf/pdf of $X$ and $Y$ is
$$f(x,y) = \frac{xy^{x-1}}{3} \text{ for }x = 1, 2, 3 \text{ and } 0 < y < 1.$$

-   Check that $\sum_{x} \int\nolimits_{-\infty}^\infty  f(x,y)dy = 1$.

-   Calculate $\mathbb{P}(2 \le X, 0.5 \le Y)$.
:::

Lastly, we'll learn about the joint cdf, which can be defined for any
random variable $X$ and $Y$.

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
**Joint cdf.**

A joint cdf is the function $F$ such that for all $(x,y) \in \bR^2$,
$$F(x,y) = \mathbb{P}(X\le x, Y \le y).$$
:::

How to go from a joint cdf to the cdf of a single random variable $X$?
Follow these steps:

$\begin{aligned}
F_X(x) & =P\{X \leq x\} \\
 & =P\{X \leq x, Y<\infty\} \\
 & =P\left(\lim _{y
\rightarrow \infty}\{X \leq x, Y \leq y\}\right) \\
 & =\lim _{y \rightarrow
\infty} P\{X \leq x, Y \leq y\} \\
 & =\lim _{y \rightarrow \infty} F(x, y) \\
 &\equiv F(x, \infty)\end{aligned}$

Here are some more properties. A joint cdf is

-   Non-decreasing for each axis (variable), when the other fixed.

-   The cdf $F_X$ of one variable $X$ can be obtained as
    $\lim_{y\to\infty} F(x,y)$.

-   If $X$ and $Y$ are continuous, the joint cdf is $\int_{-\infty}^x
      \int_{-\infty}^y f(r,s) dr \;ds$.

-   The joint pdf can be obtained by taking the second mixed partial
    derivative with respect to both variables:
    $$f_{X,Y}(x,y) = \frac{\partial^2 F(x,y)}{\partial x \partial y} = \frac{\partial^2 F(x,y)}{\partial y \partial x}$$
    at all points $(x,y)$ where the second derivative exists.

**Bivariate Normal distribution.**
